bottom_line: In 45 852 patients with suspected acute MI, metoprolol vs placebo did not significantly reduce the composite of death, reinfarction, or cardiac arrest (OR 0.96, 95% CI 0.90–1.01).
implications: These results support that, during the scheduled in-hospital treatment period, metoprolol did not significantly reduce death (OR 0.99, 0.92–1.05) or the composite of death, reinfarction, or cardiac arrest (OR 0.96, 0.90–1.01), while it did reduce reinfarction (OR 0.82, 0.72–0.92) and ventricular fibrillation (OR 0.83, 0.75–0.93) but increased cardiogenic shock (OR 1.30, 1.19–1.41). The numbers reported do not license a conclusion of an overall mortality benefit during the in-hospital treatment period, and they do show an important early safety hazard (cardiogenic shock), particularly in days 0–1.

major_points.text: Randomised placebo-controlled trial in suspected acute MI patients admitted within 24 hours.
major_points.quote: 45 852 patients admitted to 1250 hospitals within 24 h of suspected acute MI onset were randomly allocated metoprolol (up to 15 mg intravenous then 200 mg oral daily; n=22 929) or matching placebo (n=22 923).

major_points.text: Two prespecified co-primary outcomes were the composite (death, reinfarction, or cardiac arrest) and all-cause death during scheduled treatment period.
major_points.quote: The two prespeciﬁed co- primary outcomes were: (1) composite of death, reinfarction, or cardiac arrest; and (2) death from any cause during the scheduled treatment period.

major_points.text: Composite co-primary outcome was not significantly reduced with metoprolol.
major_points.quote: For death, reinfarction, or cardiac arrest, 2166 (9·4%) patients allocated metoprolol had at least one such event compared with 2261 (9·9%) allocated placebo (odds ratio [OR] 0·96, 95% CI 0·90–1·01; p=0·1).

major_points.text: All-cause death was not significantly different between groups.
major_points.quote: For death alone, there were 1774 (7·7%) deaths in the metoprolol group versus 1797 (7·8%) in the placebo group (OR 0·99, 0·92–1·05; p=0·69).

major_points.text: Metoprolol reduced reinfarction and ventricular fibrillation.
major_points.quote: Allocation to metoprolol was associated with ﬁve fewer people having reinfarction (464 [2·0%] metoprolol vs 568 [2·5%] placebo; OR 0·82, 0·72–0·92; p=0·001) and ﬁve fewer having ventricular ﬁbrillation (581 [2·5%] vs 698 [3·0%];
Overall, these reductions were counterbalanced by 11 more per 1000 developing cardiogenic shock (1141 [5·0%] vs 885 [3·9%]; OR 1·30, 1·19–1·41; p0·00001).

major_points.text: Excess cardiogenic shock occurred mainly during days 0–1 after admission.
major_points.quote: This excess of cardiogenic shock was mainly during days 0–1 after admission, whereas the reductions in reinfarction and ventricular ﬁbrillation emerged more gradually.

inclusion_criteria.text: Presented with ST elevation, left-bundle branch block, or ST depression within 24 h of symptom onset of suspected acute MI and responsible physician did not consider clear indications/contraindications to study treatments.
inclusion_criteria.quote: Patients who presented with ST elevation, left-bundle branch block, or ST depression within 24 h of the onset of the symptoms of suspected acute MI were potentially eligible for the study, provided that their responsible physician did not consider them to have clear indications for, or contraindications to, any of the study treatments.

exclusion_criteria.text: Scheduled for primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI).
exclusion_criteria.quote: Patients scheduled for primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) were to be excluded because the combined use of aspirin plus clopidogrel (or ticlopidine) was likely to be considered indicated.

baseline.characteristic: ECG abnormality at entry - ST elevation, n (%)

criticisms.text: No post-discharge follow-up was sought after first hospital discharge (or day 28).
criticisms.quote: After the ﬁrst hospital discharge (or day 28), no further follow-up was sought.

criticisms.text: Blinding could potentially be compromised because rapid blood pressure reduction could indicate active drug.
criticisms.quote: Doctors (and patients) were not asked whether they could guess the treatment allocation, but there must have been some occasions in which a rapid reduction in blood pressure correctly indicated to the doctor that active drug was being given.

criticisms.text: Trial cannot directly assess whether early excess cardiogenic shock could have been avoided by starting with oral rather than intravenous beta-blocker treatment.
criticisms.quote: The present trial cannot assess directly whether this early excess of cardiogenic shock could have been largely avoided by starting with oral rather than with intravenous -blocker treatment.
